title: Four languages
hookLine: Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan: the teaching's great languages
last: THE TEACHING ITSELF IS THE TEACHER.

lines: PUT IT IN THE PRIESTS' VERSE.
cards: The complaint comes from a pair of brothers in robes. Born brahmins, both of them, with fine speaking voices.
Monks of every name and clan and family have joined the order, they say, and each one repeats the Buddha's words in his own way of talking. The words are getting spoiled.
Their solution: put the whole teaching into the old, formal verse of the Vedas, the learned language of priests. Fixed, polished, safe. It's a reasonable request.

teach.h: HIS WORD IN ITS OWN LANGUAGE.
teach.b: That story is from the monastic rules called the Cullavagga. The Buddha rebukes the brothers, then gives a permission: the monks may learn his word in its own language. Readers have taken that line two ways.

Some read it as each monk's own language. The old commentator Buddhaghosa read it as the Buddha's own speech, which Theravada tradition calls Magadhi and identifies with Pali. The text doesn't settle it.
Either way, the teaching would not be locked in the priests' tongue. So it traveled. First, Pali, which Theravada monasteries still chant at morning and evening services.
Second, Sanskrit, in which Mahayana sutras and great Indian treatises were kept, and from which Tibetan and Chinese translators often worked. Third, Chinese.
Translators labored to find Chinese words for Indian ideas; the monk Kumarajiva's versions are still chanted in East Asian temples.
Fourth, Tibetan, into which teams of translators carried Indian texts with great care over terms. Hear it in one word.
In Pali and Sanskrit, buddha, the awakened one. In Chinese, fo, one short syllable.
In Tibetan, sangye, which Tibetan tradition says joins two ideas: cleared of what obscures, and blossomed into full knowing. One person, many sounds.
Each language also changed what people heard: a Chinese reader and a Tibetan reader meet the Buddha through different pictures.
Learning a word from each is a way of visiting their homes.

how: Theravada monasteries chant in Pali, East Asian temples chant sutras in Chinese or in local readings of Chinese, and Tibetan communities chant and study in Tibetan, while Buddhists also learn the teaching in their own everyday languages.

o: Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan, which carried the teaching
four dialects of Pali spoken in the Buddha's own day
the four Vedas, learned by the brahmins who joined the order

p: the awakened one, in Pali and Sanskrit

s: the Buddha told the two brothers to put his words into Vedic verse
he refused, and allowed the monks to learn his word in its own language.
everyone agrees what 'its own language' means in that rule
some read it as each monk's language; Buddhaghosa read it as the Buddha's own speech.
Tibetan tradition says sangye joins two ideas: cleared and blossomed
cleared of what obscures, and blossomed into full knowing.

games.q: you're the Buddha. two monks ask you to put your whole teaching into the formal verse of the Vedas. what do you say?
o: yes: fix it in the learned language.
no: learn my word in its own language.
let each monk change the teaching as he likes.
games.why: he refuses the priests' verse and allows the word in its own language. readers still debate whose language that means.

practice: On an out-breath, say softly: buddha, the awakened one, in Pali and Sanskrit. On the next, try fo, the Chinese, or sangye, the Tibetan, whichever sits easier in your mouth, and go back and forth a few times, slowly.
Then let the words go quiet, and sit with all the mouths that have said this one name in their own way.

wordCard.voice: Four languages. Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan: the great languages that carried the teaching, each giving the Buddha's word its own sound. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit buddha: the awakened one, the same word in both languages.

carryVoice: Your line: many tongues. The schools you've met this month live, in part, inside their languages. See you tomorrow.
